speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL -REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I rise not in any way to oppose the motion of my hon. friend, but rather to remind him that the government indicated some days ago that they were quite prepared to support his motion and to allow it to carry. In fact, when my hon. friend sought yesterday to have the motion carried without debate, the government acquiesced at once, and only because of an objection raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) has the motion not already carried and the reference been made to the public accounts committee. An objection having been raised to having the motion carry without debate, I feel I should say a word or two regarding the circumstances which governed the actions of the administration in having the matter referred to in the motion already inquired into.
As the house is aware, the occasion of the inquiry was the publication in Maclean's magazine, on September 1, of a sensational article entitled Canada's Armament Mysteiy. This article attracted a great deal of attention in the public press. It did not contain any charges, but it had allegations of a sort which were calculated to create suspicion with respect to the manner in which government contracts in connection with armaments and munitions were being awarded or carried out. When this article appeared inquiries were made immediately of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), of myself and others as to what we thought about it. As I recollect, the Minister of National Defence was on his way back from British Columbia to Ottawa when he was interviewed by a reporter of one of the newspapers and asked what he thought about the allegations that were made in the article. The minister replied that he thought that, as soon as parliament met, the article itself and all matters to which it referred should be made a subject of reference to the public accounts committee and the fullest possible inquiry made by the committee into the particular contract to which the article referred, namely, the contract respecting the manufacture of Bren machine guns which had been awarded to the John Inglis Company Limited. That was the minister's position the moment he saw the article.
As I have said, the article was published on September 1, and the minister reached Ottawa a few days after. When he arrived in Ottawa there was a meeting of the cabinet which he attended. He brought the matter up for the consideration of the government, and

Bren Gun-Point of Order
he felt, and other members of the government felt, that if this article with the allegations it contained were to go without investigation until parliament reassembled, which would be some time in the new year, there would immediately be created in the public mind considerable concern over these allegations and it would be assumed that the government was seeking to avoid inquiry into the matter. The government took the alternative course of not delaying for one moment the matter of instituting an inquiry, and adopted the course which would afford the most effective means for the fullest and most searching kind of inquiry, namely, an inquiry under royal commission by a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada.
I ask hon. members if it is not a fact that had there been no judicial inquiry into this matter up to this time, the government would long ere this have been charged with having waited until this parliament met before having any inquiry made into the allegations. That is undoubtedly the indictment which we would have met as soon as we assembled here, that serious charges had been made against the Department of National Defence on a matter connected with that department at a time when conditions in the world were very critical, and that we had allowed months to pass without having any inquiry made. The government felt that the matter was allimportant, in the sense that it was desirable that any ground even for suspicion concerning the conduct of the minister or any member of his staff or anything that had been done or left undone by any official of the government should be immediately known or removed and not permitted to remain a matter of conjecture. The government therefore decided to have a royal commission appointed at once.
In connection with the appointment of the royal commission I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that the government selected as the commissioner one holding such a high judicial position and so well known by the citizens of Canada generally that there could be no doubt in the mind of anyone as to the appropriateness of the appointment for an inquiry of the kind. The government made its selection from the personnel of the Supreme Court of Canada. May I also draw to the attention of the house the fact that the judge of the Supreme Court selected was not a member of the judiciary who had been appointed under a Liberal administration but one who owed his appointment to a Conservative administration, an administration of which my hon. friend the present leader of the opposition was a member. I think I am right when I say that throughout Canada generally it was felt that if the government had searched the country over, no single person, unless it were the chief justice himself, could possibly have been chosen who would have been regarded as so completely disinterested and so well qualified to perform the function of commissioner in an investigation of this kind as was Mr. Justice Davis.
The article as I say appeared on September 1. It was on September 7 that the commission was issued to Mr. Justice Davis. The commission opened its proceedings on September 19; the proceedings continued until November 24; on December 29 the report of the commissioner was presented. It was immediately translated into French, printed in both French and English, and was tabled the day after this house began its session. I ask if more expedition to have all the facts brought out in the inquiry made available to this House of Commons when parliament met, was possible.
I have mentioned the eminent suitability of Mr. Justice Davis as commissioner, and the expedition with which the whole inquiry was conducted. I should like to emphasize as well the thoroughness with which the investigation was carried on. Perhaps before indicating what Mr. Justice Davis himself felt about the thoroughness of the inquiry, I might give to the house the text of the order in council pursuant to which the commission was appointed. The order will indicate more clearly than anything else the scope of the authority which the commissioner had in conducting the inquiry. The order is dated the 7th September, 1938, and is as follows:

The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated September 7, 1938, from the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, the Prime Minister, representing that a certain Canadian periodical publication, dated September 1, 1938, contained a general article under the caption "Canada's Armament Mystery," purporting to have been prepared by Lieut.-Col. George A. Drew.
The Prime Minister observes that the author criticized some of the provisions of a certain contract executed on the 31st day of March, 1938, and tabled in parliament on the 29th day of June, 1938, made between His Majesty the King represented by the Honourable the Minister of National Defence for Canada and John Inglis Co., Limited, whereby the company undertook to furnish to His Majesty a certain supply of Bren machine guns for the use of the defence forces of Canada; numerous allegations relating to the negotiation, the terms of the contract and transactions thereunder, were made by the author as a result of which considerable public interest has since been evinced.
The Prime Minister is of opinion that a full and complete inquiry should be set on foot
Bren Gun-Point oj Order

with the least possible delay in order that the public may be fully informed of the circumstances surrounding the making of this contract and the terms thereof.
The Prime Minister, therefore, recommends that the Honourable Mr. Justice Henry Hague Davis, a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, be appointed a commissioner under Part I of the Inquiries Act to inquire fully into the preliminary discussions and negotiations leading up to and the completion of the said contract, and into the shareholdings and the transactions, if any, in the shares or securities of the said company, and the connection or activities, if any, of any member of the House of Commons in the discussions and negotiations leading up to the said contract or in the affairs of the said company or in the sale of shares or securities of the said company, and generally to inquire fully into all matters relating to the said contract and to the affairs of the said company and to the steps taken to protect the public interest; and to report upon the game.
The Prime Minister further recommends that the commissioner be authorized to engage the services of such technical advisers or other experts, clerks, reporters and assistants as he may deem necessary or advisable.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendations and submit the same for approval.
(Signed) H. W. Lothrop,
Asst. Clerk of the Privy Council.

Will the Prime Minister permit a question?
Mr. MACKENZIE KING; Yes.

Did the commission which was issued follow in exact terms the last half of that order in council? Without discussion, I would just say that the commissioner's attention would not be directed to the order in council but rather to the terms of the commission issued to him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not the commission before me, but I should think it would have followed the terms of the order in council. If it did not, I shall read to my hon. friend in a moment a letter which I personally sent to the commissioner at the time I transmitted to him a copy of the order in council appointing him a commissioner. The letter made clear to Mr. Justice Davis that if in the course of the inquiry any more latitude were required for investigation of any phase of the matter, the government would see that it was accorded to him, and if necessary to this end, his commission would be amended accordingly.
When the order in council was passed, the matter being one of great public interest, I released to the press from the office of the Prime Minister a statement making perfectly clear the desire of the government that the inquiry should be as complete, comprehensive and thorough as it was possible to make it. The statement I think appeared in all the

papers of the country, but I shall read it to hon. members in order to refresh their memories:
On Thursday last the Honourable Mr. Mackenzie, Minister of National Defence, on behalf of the government, announced that a royal commission would be appointed to undertake as soon as possible an inquiry into the allegations made by Colonel George Drew in Maclean's Magazine of September 1st, regarding the contract made by the National Defence department with the John Inglis Company of Toronto for the manufacture of Bren guns.
At the request of the Prime Minister, Mr. Justice Davis of the Supreme Court of Canada, has agreed to undertake the inquiry. Mr. Justice Davis has done so on the understanding that he receive only his out-of-pocket expenses.
The Honourable J. I,. Ralston has been retained as counsel for the government to assist the commission.
The reference to the commission, while it does not specifically mention the article in Maclean's magazine, has been made broad enough to cover all of Colonel Drew's allegations, as set forth therein. This being its purpose, should it appear to the commissioner in the course of his inquiry that the terms or wording of the reference are to this end inadequate in any particular, the reference will be enlarged as, in the opinion of the commissioner, will serve adequately to meet its intended purpose.
The government hopes Colonel Drew will appear before the commission and give all the assistance he can in substantiation of his allegations. Further, the government would be prepared to pay the reasonable expenses and remuneration of counsel for Colonel Drew, should he wish to engage counsel to assist him.
As soon as the preliminary work of organization of the commission is completed, the inquiry will commence. This, it is expected, will be not later than the 19th instant.
In the troubled world of to-day, the Canadian people reluctantly have shouldered what is, for them, a very considerable burden, for the purpose of national defence. The Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence, and the government as a whole, desire that in all the defence measures that may be taken by the government, not only shall there be no wrongdoing, but no suspicion of wrongdoing. The Canadian people are entitled to this. The article published by Colonel Drew cannot but create suspicion on these matters in the minds of the Canadian people. For this reason the government desires that the inquiry be conducted as expeditiously and as thoroughly as possible.

Colonel Ralston was appointed by the government to assist the commission. Colonel Ralston also regarded the matter as one of public duty at a time of great concern in the country, and he also agreed to act as counsel to assist the commission, but only on the condition that he would not be given any honorarium or remuneration for his professional services but allowed simply such expenses or disbursements as might be incurred in the course of the inquiry.
The letter I wrote Mr. Justice Davis was as follows:
Office of the Prime Minister Canada
Ottawa, September 8, 1938. The Honourable Mr. Justice Davis,
361 Mariposa Road,
Roekcliffe,
Ottawa, Ontario.
My dear Mr. Justice Davis:
I have pleasure in enclosing a copy of order in council P.C. 2251, covering your appointment as a commissioner to inquire fully into the circumstances of the contract with the John Inglis Company for the supply of Bren machine guns for the use of the defence forces of Canada. I enclose, as well, a copy of the statement given to the press following the meeting of the cabinet yesterday.
I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to express the deep appreciation of my colleagues and myself of your willingness to undertake this public duty. I need scarcely add that you will have the full support and cooperation of the government w'hich, above all else, desires that the inquiry be carried out in a manner which will meet with the entire approval of the Canadian people.

The reply by Mr. Justice Davis to this communication was as follows:
Judges' Chambers Supreme Court,
Ottawa
September 10th, 1938. The Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
My dear Mr. Prime Minister,
Your letter of the 8th instant, enclosing a copy of order in council P.C. 2251 covering my appointment as a commissioner to inquire fully into the Bren machine guns contract, as well as a copy of the statement given to the press, have been duly received.
I particularly note your assurance of the full support and cooperation of the government in the work of the commission and please accept my assurance that I do value the expression of the appreciation of yourself and your colleagues in my undertaking the work.
I was made fully aware by Mr. Crerar on your behalf of the government's attitude in the whole matter before accepting the commission and it was such that it became, with the full concurrence of the chief justice of the court, my plain duty to accede to your request under the special circumstances.
Yours very truly,
H. H. Davis.
The reference to my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) in that letter arises from the fact that my colleague was acting Prime Minister during part of the time I unfortunately was indisposed, when this matter first came up. At my request he went to confer with Mr. Justice Davis and with the chief justice with respect to securing, if possible, the services of Mr. Justice Davis for the work of the commission.
Just here I should like to say how much the government appreciated Mr. Justice Davis undertaking this task as a public duty, and also the kindness of the chief justice, the Right Hon. Sir Lyman Duff, in allowing one of the members of his court, at a time when the court was pressed in its work, to give the necessary time to conduct this all-important inquiry. Both the chief justice and Mr. Justice Davis were actuated, I know, by the highest motives of public service, and I think I should express to each of them the appreciation not only of the government but of this house in not having hesitated to inconvenience themselves to the extent they did in being prepared to have the work of the commission taken on by a member of the court as well as for the valuable public service which was thereby performed.
What I have read indicates, I believe, as clearly as anything possibly could that it would have been impossible to have given any commissioner more complete authority to inquire into every phase and aspect of a situation than was given to Mr. Justice Davis.

I think there is no question but that the commissioner so understood his powers, and that he conducted the inquiry in a manner which would enable him to say to the government that the whole task had been performed very thoroughly. I should like to read what Mr. Justice Davis himself has said with respect to the thorough manner in which the [DOT] inquiry was conducted. The house has before it the report of the royal commission on the Bren machine gun contract, and at page 4 bon. members will find the following statement by Mr. Justice Davis:
The commission opened on September 19, 1938, and concluded on Thursday, November 24, 1938. The taking of testimony and the argument of counsel occupied thirty-six days. With the exception of Major General Caldwell (then master general of the ordnance) of the Department of National Defence, whose illness prevented his being examined at any time during the sittings of the commission, every one who it was thought might be able to throw light on the subject of the inquiry gave testimony voluntarily.
It was not necessary to issue a single subpoena to enforce the attendance of any witness. Your commissioner is satisfied that all available documents in any way relevant and material to the subject matter of the inquiry were presented to the commission.
And later, at page 52, in the concluding portions of the report Mr. Justice Davis emphasizes again the complete nature of the inquiry, in the following words:
All the sittings of the commission were public and your commissioner was pleased to hear counsel characterize the inquiry at its close, as "a most searching and thorough inquiry."
Just in passing I should like to direct attention to the words of the commissioner wherein lie states that all the sittings of the commission were public. In so doing I must refer to the somewhat hasty remarks made yesterday by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) when he said that in having the matter referred to the public accounts committee it was being referred to some " packed committee " which would hold its proceedings behind closed doors. I was pleased to notice my hon. friend felt he had used an exaggerated and unwarranted phrase at the time, and withdrew it. The point I wish to make clear at this time is that the public accounts committee does not operate behind closed doors. The inquiry by the committee will be as much in the open as was the inquiry before Mr. Justice Davis.
Further, I would point out with respect to the composition of the committee that, so far as representation from the different sides of the house is concerned, it will be precisely the same proportions and follow the same rules as have been followed in setting up all committees in previous sessions and in all parliaments.

There is only one other matter to which I should like to refer-because I do not think this is the occasion on which to debate any phases of the report. My opinion is that matters therein referred to come up more properly at other times. The motion now before us has regard to the reference of the John Inglis Company contract, and one or two other matters, to the committee on public accounts. Inasmuch, however, as the leader of the opposition has indicated that it is desirable to have a debate on the motion in its present form, nothwithstanding the acceptance by the government of the motion in its entirety, and the fact, as has been already pointed out, that part of what is requested in the motion has already been met through the tabling of certain reports and their reference to the public accounts committee, I believe I should at once read to the house what the commissioner has to say with respect to the conduct of the Minister of National Defence, the conduct of officials in the minister's department and of others of the public service whose action in some particular would seem to have been called in question by the allegations in the article which occasioned the appointment of the commission.
I direct the attention of the house to what is said at page 51 of the report. Before reading may I repeat that the commissioner indicated nothing had been left undone which he thought could have been done, that the inquiry was as searching as it possibly could be, and that everything which was considered relevant was fully inquired into. The commissioner says:
There is no evidence that any member of the Senate or of the House of Commons of Canada was admitted to any share or part of the contract, or to any benefits to arise therefrom, or had been promised or given any suggestion that he was to have any share or part of the contract or was to be admitted to any share or part of the contract, or to any benefit to arise from the contract.
Then a little farther on he says:
There is no evidence that any senator or member had any connection with or took any part in the affairs of the company or in the sale of shares or securities of the company.
I think it right to say that there is no evidence (nor is there in the evidence any ground for suspicion) that the minister or the deputy minister or any officer or official of the Department of National Defence was guilty of any act of corruption or anything in the nature of corruption.
I have felt it desirable to place this quotation from the report before hon. members, particularly because of the intimation made by the leader of the opposition that despite

its acceptance by the government we are to have a debate on the motion at the present time.
May I conclude my observations by drawing the attention of hon. members to the rules of the house with respect to committees appointed to inquire into particular matters. I raise the point I do because I believe it suggests something that possibly the leader of the opposition as well as many other hon. members may have overlooked. It is a point which I believe is important to bring to their attention before the debate proceeds further. Subsection 2 of standing order 63 with respect to select special committees of the house, as it appears in Beauchesne's parliamentary rules and forms, is as follows:
It shall always be understood that no member who declares or decides against the principle of a bill, resolution, or matter to be committed, can be nominated of such committee.
Citation No. 625, which is explanatory of the rule, is as follows:
The term "select" committee, is usually applied to designate a committee appointed to consider a particular subject, on the occurrence of the occasion for its appointment, as where a committee is appointed to consider a petition or memorial, or to make inquiries into a particular subject. Select committees are sometimes turned into standing committees by subsequent references to them relating to the same subject.
I am aware, Mr. Speaker, that the committee on public accounts is not a select special committee, but that it is one of the standing committees of the house. As I have just indicated, however, a select special committee may become a standing committee. I submit, however, that the principle is precisely the same with respect to what should govern the action of hon. members in discussing a matter which is being referred to any committee, for purposes of investigation and adjudication.
The public accounts committee will have in its membership several hon. members of the house and, when this motion carries, the committee will have referred to it the contract in question and matters relevant thereto. Each hon. member of the committee will be expected, on his honour, to investigate fully the matter which has been referred to the committee of which he is a member. He will be expected, as one who is privileged to sit on the committee, to form his judgment with respect to what should be reported to the house. The house in turn will be expected to consider, with the regard that is due a report coming from the public accounts committee, what is sent to it by members of that committee as a result of the special opportunity they have had to inquire into all aspects of the matter referred to them.

The point I am raising for consideration at the moment is whether hon. members have considered their position in entering into a debate at the present time on a matter that is to be referred to the public accounts committee and possibly determining by the remarks that they may make what their attitude will be in that committee, thereby prejudging the whole matter. What I am concerned about is that some other hon. members in the course of debate at this stage may without realizing the significance of their actions commit themselves by their expressions to such an extent that every man, woman and child in this country will know that they have arrived at a particular attitude which they intend to maintain in the committee, and that the committee therefore would lose in the public mind if not also in fact the judicial aspect which it ought to have.
I think that the matter is sufficiently clear. As I say, if it were a special committee of the house being appointed for this purpose and to which this reference was being made, no hon. member who had expressed views in this house which prejudged the situation would be entitled to sit on that committee. I submit that in this particular case, seeing that the reference is specific, the public accounts committee is, as regards the position of those who may serve on it, very much in the same position as if the reference had been to a special committee. The underlying principle is the same. I regard the matter as being sufficiently serious to warrant a step which will enable hon. members to consider their attitudes carefully before they begin to speak in the course of the debate. In order to give them that opportunity I propose to move the adjournment of the debate with a view to having it continued on Monday next instead of proceeded with this afternoon, and I move accordingly.

The minister is correct. I do not wish to befog the issue or to misconstrue the intention of the premier of Nova Scotia. Fifty per cent is also put up, which makes $40,000 in all. But even taking that, it would not give a week's work to the fishermen, and then they would have to use that money to live. They desire to go lobster-fishing, on the first day of March, four miles off the coast, and they have not the traps, nor the anchors or the floats. They must go into the woods and cut trees; laths, nails, corks, and so on, must be bought. They must paint their traps and get things ready so that when the weather becomes milder they can take up their vocation again. When I tell you that in that storm over 100,000 lobster traps were absolutely destroyed, 44,000 in Yarmouth and Digby alone, and in Lunenburg and Queens and in the western part of Halifax, 100,000 traps, 200,000 buoys and 100,000 floats; when you consider the dire want of these people, their worry in face of these conditions, and so on, you will appreciate the appeal that I make.

Some people have said to me in defence of a policy in which I do not concur, "Well, the fishermen have not said very much about it." No, they go their weary way; and with this great gale many of them went down in their boats, there to remain until the final judgment day when they shall arise from the bottom of the deep to appear before their God. This is not a matter that should be treated lightly, and I am sure the Minister of Fisheries desires to do his part. The same can be said of the Prime Minister, because there is no hon. gentleman sitting in this house who has a more human heart than the Prime Minister. In making this appeal I ask that serious and immediate consideration be given by direct contribution, not by putting money in the hands of the fishermen, but through the materials necessary to enable them to make their pots, gear and other equipment, so that between now and the first of March they can get that equipment into shape to begin their work.
I wish to thank the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) for the manner in which he expressed himself this afternoon in this house, for his sympathy with the plight of the fishermen. I wish also to thank the Minister of Labour for his contribution, but it is not idequate. The money I believe is available in the fisheries department to-day to put up seventy-five per cent in cash under present legislation, as a gift, not by way of loan; the remaining twenty-five per cent to come from the province of Nova Scotia. There are only two roads open in reference to this matter. One road leads to success, bringing happiness to the homes of the fishermen through conditions of life that are bearable, and eliminating in some degree suffering and want. The other road leads to political oblivion for those who stand in the way. One of these two courses must be pursued.
I do not mention this with any reference to the present government of which I am an enthusiastic supporter. When this urgent condition exists, as it does, and for some reason unknown there is an attitude which is not in harmony with the finer qualities of the human heart, then I say that if necessary we should interpret section 91 of the British North America Act which defines the federal powers and recognize the "fisheries" as a matter that comes under the federal jurisdiction. We should not draw fine distinctions between fisheries and fishermen. There is no difference between fisheries and fishermen when a fisherman is found with undersized lobsters in his possession; that is. not regarded as a matter to be prosecuted by the provincial authority, but is dealt with by the federal

authority on the report of their inspector, and by the magistrates in Nova Scotia. If a fisherman is liable to penalties for breach of regulations made by federal authority under the Fisheries Act, then I say it is too fine a distinction, a distinction without a difference, to say that fishermen are not part of fisheries and therefore it is not possible for the federal Department of Fisheries to deal with this matter solely but only in cooperation with the Nova Scotia government.
In conclusion, I thank you, sir, and thank hon. members of the house on all sides, because I do believe, have believed all my life, that when the human heart is touched there is an immediate and automatic response. The conditions in my constituency are as I have described them. I shall not undertake to speak in more than a general way, because this motion is not debatable. But last evening the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier) said that this matter could not be dealt with except by direct aid through proper channels, and he intimated through the municipal councils. I agree with that. It showed a sympathetic interest on his part, and sympathetic interest was shown by the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of National Revenue who came to my aid. And when I have the Minister of National Defence behind me it is not a Bren gun, but a man in the real sense of the word, and when the Bren gun is fired the report will sound from one end of Canada to the other and will result in only one thing. I hope I am not going to be on that committee because I might be biased, but the opposition will find that our powder was dry and that the Bren gun will be fired if the occasion arises. I hope the occasion will not arise.

In the early part of December a storm of unusual severity struck the Atlantic coast, not only of Nova Scotia but of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick; and on the western coast of Nova Scotia it was particularly severe. The result was that the fishing

gear of the lobster fishermen, who had their traps in the water just a few days, suffered extensive destruction. As soon as the storm subsided, instructions were given the officers of the department to make a survey of the situation and report the extent of the damage and the extent to which the fishermen were affected. So far as Nova Scotia is concerned, after several daj's of survey and checking and re-checking, the total damage was estimated at somewhere between $100,000 and $125,000 representing destruction of boats and gear, but the major part being in the destruction of lobster traps.
The obligation concerning fishermen, their persons and property, has always been understood and interpreted, by those who preceded me in the department ever since it came into existence, to be primarily a provincial obligation. Since this parliament, for the last three years at least, has deemed it advisable by supplementary appropriations to grant sums of money to help reestablish needy fishermen in their occupations, these moneys have always been distributed under agreements entered into with the provinces concerned. The provinces recognized their primary liability and accepted the money voted by parliament simply as a contribution to help them discharge this obligation.

I am sure this house will agree that is the most that can be done by the government or this house unless the terms of the appropriation are changed and we are allowed to expend the money for purposes other than those for which it was voted. Unless that is done the hands of the Department of Fisheries are tied; we cannot touch that money which is in the treasury. However, the treasury of the dominion has been tapped; in other words money has been offered to the province of Nova Scotia with which they claim they can meet the situation and remedy the conditions complained of, in the manner they have selected.
So far the Department of Fisheries has never dealt directly with individuals as long as the provincial authorities recognized their responsibility and were willing to cooperate with us in disbursing the moneys voted by parliament. Of course we always made it a condition that they should supplement with money of their own the amounts appropriated by parliament, because theirs was the responsibility and we did not want them to run away with the idea that the responsibility was ours. We have not taken the legal, technical attitude; we have never tried to take refuge behind the terms of the British North America Act. Whenever a disaster has occurred of national importance, or of such magnitude that the provinces could not either borrow the necessary money or obtain credit in order to meet the situation, as the house well knows, the dominion government has always helped the provinces. The province of Nova Scotia stands in no different position. Our attitude toward that province is no different from what it has been toward other provinces. If we are told that the province is not in a position to help those people, it will be our duty to consider whether or not

we should step over their heads and deal directly with the individuals.
That is the situation, placed before the house as briefly as I could put it. I hope negotiations will continue, that the situation of those people who have suffered and who are greatly handicapped will be corrected, and that they will be placed in a position where, when the next fishing season opens, they can earn their livelihood as they have done in the past.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE-LOSS OF LOBSTER TRAPS AND EQUIPMENT ON WESTERN COAST OF NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject is one
which is veiy interesting to me because I believe I am personally familiar with every port and village along that coast. This is not the first time that violent tempests have swept the coast and caused grave destruction of, shall I say, the plant necessary to carry on lobster and other types of fishing. But I believe the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) has shown, by the confused manner in which he has discussed the subject, that he is labouring under very great difficulties in explaining the government's neglect in this particular instance. The hon. member is one for whom I have very high esteem. He is a graduate of my own university, and he certainly could not have passed the examination so well as he did in that university without knowing that the sea coast and inland fisheries are under the exclusive jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada.
This parliament has made many innovations and many irruptions into provincial rights by voting large sums of money which I have thought were beyond the power of parliament to vote, for the purpose of carrying on services which are peculiarly and necessarily-I might . say exclusively-provincial. Section 91 of the British North America Act makes the situation clear. I shall not quote the whole section but only the part pertinent to the matter before us:
... It is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say-
And going down to item No. 12:
12. Sea coast and inland fisheries.

Certainly parliament may properly vote any sums of money which are necessary or deemed expedient with regard to a service over which it has absolute control. That, I suggest, cannot be controverted.
Now, why all this worry about negotiations with the provincial government? Here is a great calamity which has overtaken one of the sea coast fisheries of Nova Scotia, resulting, as the minister has said, in the destruction, to the extent of $150,000 in value, of the implements necessary to the fisherman in carrying on his vocation. It is admitted clearly by the minister that the fishermen themselves have not the means to replace the necessary plant and equipment which have been destroyed. If it had been a calamity which had overtaken some other country, such as one which occurred recently in Chile, we could, as we have in times past, under an assumption of authority, and for the sake of overcoming the results of a. great disaster, vote sums of money to relieve a foreign people engaged in a foreign industry over which we have no legislative control.

But here is a case in respect of which clearly and plainly parliament has legislative jurisdiction. It has within its power the right to vote moneys to sustain this industry in any way parliament may deem advisable. Therefore, why labour the discussion by bringing in votes which have been made on the motion of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) to assist in road building in Nova Scotia, a project over which we have no control and with which, according to our legislative jurisdiction, we have nothing to do? Why bring in confusing discussions about road grants when parliament, and particularly the government, which is the executive committee of parliament, is face to face with the results of a great disaster which has overtaken the people engaged in fishing on that southern coast of Nova Scotia?
It is true that parliament may not have voted moneys in the past because it was not anticipating a calamity of that extent. It may be true that last session no appropriation was made which could properly be devoted to the purposes suggested. But that vote of last session is not the only remedy. This calamity occurred long before this parliament
met. The facts were known by the minister at least two months ago, if my memory is correct. He had investigations made and he knew the facts then. Grants could have been made by a special order of the governor in council to relieve the distress in a temporary and preliminary manner until such time as parliament could meet to deal adequately with the matter. Parliament has now met, and I suggest there is no reason in the world why, being cognizant of the facts, there should be any excuse for delay in parliament giving the necessary relief by appropriating by a vote, outright, the moneys necessary to reestablish these fishermen, if such procedure is deemed advisable. The minister has very frankly stated his views as to the extent of the disaster. Parliament certainly should provide, by some measure, adequate advances to these men to enable them to reestablish themselves before the next fishing season.
I have not consulted the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) about this, but I believe hon. members on this side would be willing to support a vote sufficient to relieve the fishermen who suffered such destructive damage. At any rate I have a strong and friendly feeling for the hon. member, and I am glad to be able to support his proposal. My knowledge of Nova Scotia comes from various visits to that province where, as in the other provinces of the maritimes, the beautiful countryside and the kindly, charming and hospitable people have won my heart on many occasions. I believe I have visited the maritimes ten or a dozen times, and always I have come back thinking highly of those provinces and realizing fully why they have given so much to the cultural, the educational, and, in general, the highest life of this great dominion.
To get to the subject in a rather general way, when I was in the maritimes on the last occasion, I believe in September or October, although I do not recall the exact period, the question of the condition of the fishermen in the maritimes and particularly in Nova Scotia was prominent in the press and on the lips of the people. Indeed there was quite a row going on down there, in which, I am sorry to say, I took no part. It was a row between those who said the conditions of the fishermen were very bad and those who, apparently, contended they were not so bad. Being, as I have said, of the same extraction as the senior member for Halifax, I naturally favour the under-dog anyway, and I found myself entirely in accord and sympathy with the writers-some from Ontario, some from Halifax and other parts of Nova Scotia-who took the side of the fishermen in dire want, so it was said, in the various ports of that province.
The other day I had a letter from a friend with whom I have corresponded a good deal, an outstanding man in Nova Scotia who has been taking a strong attitude with respect to the needs of the fishermen. He is one of those who do not agree that there is too much maudlin sympathy extended to these fishermen, and I must confess that in large measure my sympathy for them has been the results of the educational effect he has had

upon me. He wrote to me before this incident occurred; at any rate his letter had no reference to the question which is now under discussion in this house. He informed me that some of the fishermen of Nova Scotia earned only S50 per annum after paying cost of gas and bait. In other districts they received from $100 to $150, while in the better localities their earnings amounted to about $400. I know nothing about the facts, but I do know a great deal about my correspondent, and I can assure the house that he 'keeps himself well posted upon all subjects that relate to the welfare of those delightful provinces by the sea. I am sure he is correct in the information he has given me. My hon. friend nods his head. I listened to him carefully and I must admit that I knew more about the subject after hearing the senior member for Halifax. There seemed to be some controversy, but I could follow the senior member for Halifax rather better. I have no doubt, however, that both hon. gentlemen representing that constituency are equally sympathetic to the fishermen there.
On this question there seems to be more unanimity in all parts of the house than is usual on matters of this sort. As the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George pointed out, we are prone continually to take a deep interest in the condition of people in remote parts of the world. We readily throw up our hands in horror at some catastrophe in some far away land, and very often I have seen us collect money for floods in China, for example, as the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) points out, have money voted by parliament. Since, therefore, everyone seems agreed on this question, I should like to see the minister give the assistance asked for. He would certainly get the support of this entire party if he decided to give at the earliest possible moment this much-needed aid to people who are our fel-Iow-Canadians. Sometimes I am ashamed to think of the riches we possess when I reflect upon the extreme want that exists in some parts of the country, and though my hon. friends to my left take, in my opinion, a radical view of some matters I confess that I sometimes find myself sympathizing with them. In this rich country of ours with our immense resources, a huge area with a small population, it does seem strange that there should be so many people in want. Anything that is done by this government, anything that is done by the minister on this occasion, will receive the support of the party with which I am associated.
When I was in Nova Scotia I heard a great deal about the work done by the cooperatives,

The discussion has taken a somewhat wider range than I expected it would when I said that in my opinion the matter was one of urgent public importance. The reason that I supported the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) in moving the adjournment of the house was that I knew, as other members from Nova Scotia know, of the storm that took place a few months ago and the damage that was done. The extent of the damage has not been definitely ascertained, but it is supposed to be in the neighbourhood of 8125,000. It has been intimated to me that it does not exceed $100,000, though it may be more than that. While it is not definitely, it is approximately ascertainable.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier) has told of the distribution of the damage. Unfortunately for his constituency the greater part of it is in Shelburne and Yarmouth with some in Clare and Digby. His constituency is by 'far the greatest sufferer. The house is disposed to be sympathetic; the government is disposed to be sympathetic; and all members of this parliament as well as members of the legislatures of the maritime provinces realize that the	income	received by	fishermen	on theAtlantic coast of Nova Scotia is very low. Conditions among these people have been a matter of concern to the Minister of Fisheries and	to the	government	from the	time it
assumed office.
I do not think the immediate question is primarily a constitutional one, nor is it a question whether we are sympathetic with the fishermen, because we are. The immediate question is a practical one. As the hon. member	for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare	pointedout, these fishermen at the present time are not	engaged	in fishing;	they will	not be
engaged in fishing until March 1. They find that in some districts one-third, in other districts one-quarter, of their traps were destroyed by this storm. The question is how to help them reestablish themselves. Two views are expressed as to the method we should adopt: One view is that we should resort to direct relief; the other is that indirect relief is the better method. It seems to me that the issue is just as simple as that. Is this an occasion for the administration of indirect relief or direct relief? The province will do everything it can, I am satisfied, and this

government will do everything it can, I can assure the house. The question is as to the method to be followed.
Whatever the constitutional position is- and I must say I never before heard the view expressed that was enunciated by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) to-day; this particular kind of situation has always been regarded as one to be dealt with by the provincial authorities- but whatever the constitutional position, we must work in cooperation with the provincial government in a case of this kind. This government did so in the case of New Brunswick; it did so in the case of Prince Edward Island, and it must do so in the case of Nova Scotia. Even if it were a government of which we disapproved we would do so; if we were dealing with a premier whom we did not like we would do so; but where we are working with friends in whom we have confidence there is certainly no reason why we should work at cross-purposes with the government of Nova Scotia. Therefore we must examine with respect and with care the proposals of the government of Nova Scotia. That government has its men on the ground; it has its local members to consult, who know conditions there, and they have come to the conclusion that the best way to deal with this situation is by indirect instead of by direct relief. The premier of Nova Scotia proposes to spend a substantial sum of money on work in these very districts, so that these very men who have lost their gear will have an income from which they can make good their losses. Perhaps the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare did not say it, but I can say that men are at work at the present time. The premier of Nova Scotia tells me that 750 men will be at work next week and that this number will probably be increased as the necessities of the case require.
I am like the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare in that I find it difficult to sit silent when I hear hostile criticism of the premier of Nova Scotia. His qualities of heart and mind are well known not only in Nova Scotia but all through Canada. I know of the attention he has given to this matter, the study he has given it, and I know of his deep human sympathy in this situation. When, after his study, he says that the best way of dealing with it, having in mind his and our responsibilities and the future, is by instituting a works program through these districts so that these men will be able to earn money with which to replenish their gear, I do not think we should break the rule that has been followed since confederation and step in and-

I am not criticizing the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) for bringing this matter up or expressing his views; I am not criticizing the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare for holding certain views in the matter, but the situation is being dealt with carefully, sympathetically and sincerely, and, I think, in a practical manner. It may be that further developments will cause some change to be made in the present arrangements, or some addition to be made to the expenditure. It may be that we shall find some way to use part of the fisheries vote which the minister says he has been advised is not available for assistance in road work. Money has been paid to the government of Nova Scotia to assist, not only the $20,000 mentioned, but $50,000 before that; it was before the storm but nevertheless $50,000 of a special grant of assistance was paid to Nova Scotia, and I can assure the house on behalf of the government that we shall do our best to work out ways and means of meeting the situation, in cooperation with our friends in the province in whom we have confidence.

I am deeply interested in this problem. I am also deeply interested in the way it is proposed to spend this money. I am inclined to sympathize with the proposal of the hon. .member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier) that there should be a direct issue 71492-39
to the men concerned of half of the cost of the traps. At the same time I have of course no desire to interfere with the administration of Nova Scotia by the premier of that province. But two or three things come to my mind as a result of experience I have had with similar situations. We in the west have been sufferers for a long time and have learned something about relief, direct and indirect. I gather from the remarks of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) that it will be necessary to put into the hands of these sufferers at least $63,000 to enable them to procure the $125,000 worth of traps which they have lost. I understand from the remarks of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare that half the cost of the traps is for material and the rest represents labour which the fisherman himself can contribute. I gather then that there must be $63,000 issued to the sufferers.
The first thing I wonder about is this: Will each of these men who suffered a loss find himself able to obtain work on these road projects? If there is any considerable number who for any reason whatever will find the work not available to them, then the effort to give them relief is not going to effect its purpose; there still will be a good many sufferers. I have seen this, in similar cases, work out many times in my own constituency and my own province. It is going to be an exceedingly difficult matter to devise and design a road project of such a kind and in such a geographical location that it will make available to each of the sufferers along that long seacoast sufficient work to enable him to earn enough, net, to buy his traps. That is the first serious difficulty in the way of the indirect relief proposal.
There is another matter which has been forced upon my mind through experience. We may design a works project; we may say, "Now, we are going to spend so much on this road," and we assume that a certain part of that money will go into the hands of the labourers. It not infrequently works out that after the road is planned we put on a number of high class machines which eat up a great deal of the money in gasoline and repairs of various kinds, and which also displace a large number of the very men whom the project was designed to assist. We have learned in my province in three or four years a great deal regarding this matter. I might just give an illustration. When we set out to build roads we hired men, teams and scrapers and let them build the roads. Then we found that the roads which were built, compared with the roads constructed with modem, high class machinery, were very expensive, and the

There may be some who fancy I have had no experience in these matters, but I have had a little. I know there are all kinds of machines. Last night I saw pictures of a wonderful machine which I thought could never work. I never knew they had a machine that could go through a forest and prepare the way for back-fires, until I saw the picture of such a machine last night. In these days they have machines that will do nearly everything, but the men do not get the work. That is a serious matter, which I would draw to the attention of hon. members, because it might result in the expenditure of this money not achieving ihe desired object.
Then there is another matter. If these men live at a considerable distance from the proposed roads it is of vital importance that we know whether or not their transportation expenses to the project and back home again are to be borne by the men employing them or by themselves. If those expenses are to be borne by the sufferers, then those who live fifty or sixty miles away from the proposed projects will use up all their earnings in transportation costs and will not have sufficient left to enable them to accomplish the object we had in mind in designing the work.
There is another thing that frequently eats up the money. Sometimes when the road project is planned we allow the cost of material, machinery, and all that kind of thing, to be taken out. Then, from the standpoint of the men, there is another fact. When the men get to the work, are they to be provided with board and lodging? I have known some of the most glaring injustices to result from a situation such as this: A man would be told that he would receive so much an hour. After he had reached the scene of the activity, after paying his transportation cost, he would be told that he had to pay so much a day for his board, so much a day for his lodging, and sometimes so much a day for his blankets, the result being that what the

man had left over would hardly keep him in chewing-gum.
All these matters have to be considered, I believe, in connection with this project. While I am speaking I wish to express, through the members who represent the sufferers, my group's deepest sympathy with them in their sore trial, and I should be pleased if the hon. members would convey that expression to these people. We westerners have had plenty of suffering; we know what it is. We appreciate the courage the people in the east have always shown. We realize there are no finer people in the Dominion of Canada than they. Now that their turn has come to suffer, we hasten to lend our support to whatever measures and whatever expenditures this parliament may find necessary in order to supply them with adequate means of fitting themselves to gain a livelihood. I personally will support any proposal the minister may see fit to introduce, as will my group, and we can speak for the whole of the people of Alberta, whose sympathy will be right with those who are stricken. But I should like to feel sure that the money is going to get into the hands of the people who need it, and not into the hands of a number of people who will try to get jobs, such as contractors, sub-contractors, sub-sub-contractors, timekeepers and the like, all of whom, as we know from bitter experience, somehow do manage to figure in altogether too many propositions of this kind.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this question we seem to find a spirit of harmony and accord in reference to the desirability and the need of doing something effective for those who suffered in this disaster. I think we might go one step further and say it is generally recognized that a disaster has occurred which is out of the ordinary, and that it is not a matter of day-to-day routine in connection with this most unfortunate question of relief.
Looking at it, therefore, from that angle, I ask myself the question: What is the best thing to do under the circumstances? As the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) who has just taken his seat has asked: What is the most effective way in which we can render help? I have a good deal of respect for the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley), particularly for his native fairness in expressing himself. At the moment, however, I find myself in direct opposition to his view when he says that this is peculiarly a provincial matter. The fact that it happens to be on the coast of Nova Scotia geographically makes it provincial. But from the point of view of administration I am inclined to agree

Fishing Industry-Lobster Traps
with the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Cahan) that it comes within the direct purview of the dominion authorities. In other words, it is of a nature where we as a parliament may deal directly with it.
I agree with the Minister of National Revenue that so far as possible in all such matters we should act in harmony with the provincial governments. I have no desire or disposition to criticize the provincial government, nor must anything I shall say be interpreted as any reflection upon the premier of Nova Scotia or the government of that province. But before making a suggestion I should like to review briefly the two suggested methods of assistance, roads or traps. If we adopt the method of helping these men and their families by road work, it seems to me that a danger arises. The men must live while they are working on the roads. Any work on the roads given by way of relief, of which I have known in Canada, has resulted in very little more being given to the individual than merely enough to live through the period of time during which he has actually been engaged on the work. In other words, I do not think we should assume for a moment that a man will save enough out of the small wages he may get on road work to reequip him in his industry, and supply him with the instruments to carry on his work. I think there is^ a very grave danger in following that course in this instance.
I shall not repeat the arguments or the suggestion of the hon. member who has just spoken, but so far as helping the lobster fishermen who have suffered from the disaster by giving them road work is concerned, I must say I think it would be a mistake. Let us see what they require. Hon. members opposite will correct me if I am wrong. Usually these lobster traps are set out-I believe that is the term. In this disastrous storm many were swept away. In other words, the instruments used by the fishermen for their daily toil have been destroyed. They are lost-gone. The main object we should have in mind is to replace the instrument which has been lost, or, in other words, to reinstate them in their normal positions as lobster fishermen. That, I believe, is what we are aiming at. I suggest, therefore, that if we could supply the lobster fisherman with the equipment peculiar to his vocation as a fisherman we would be doing him more good than by giving him a job on the road. *
Here is another thought: We will assume the road work is to be done by hand work, and that no machinery will be used. Every man would have to have a wheelbarrow, a shovel 'and a pick. I venture to say that the wheel-71492- 39J
barrow, shovel and pick would make up a substantial portion of the cost of restoring his fishing equipment. I say it would be far better to spend our money on equipment he could use in gaining his livelihood, rather than on equipment for road work. I am going to suggest, without any intention of expressing an opinion different from that of the province, that we should allow the province to give whatever relief it wishes, by way of road work or in any other manner it may choose, and that in this instance the federal government should go directly, as it has the power to do,-in fact I think it should do it as a duty-to the assistance of the fishermen, by supplying them with new equipment to replace that which has been lost and, if necessary, in addition to that give them such further relief as may be required.
The suggestion has been made that the assistance. will not be required until March. I look at the calendar and I see that to-day is February 3. It will be only a very short time until March. By the time the money is granted, distributed and in their hands the first of March will be upon us.
Another point to be remembered when speaking of fisheries is this. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth - Clare (Mr. Pottier) said it was the custom to fish in November and December; then in January and February to lay off because of prevailing stormy weather, and then to begin again on March I. Knowing something about the habits of fishermen, I know it is essential that the moment fine weather comes they be in a position to take advantage of it, so that there is no time to be lost in rendering this assistance as early as possible.
I make the suggestion that as a parliament we should give the assistance direct. I would suggest that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who is now in his seat, should bring down a supplementary estimate in the current year 1938-39, which does not expire until March 31, *-he could bring it down tomorrow, if he wished-wherein he would make a definite and direct grant to be expended for the assistance of these fishermen.
There is no doubt that the livelihood of these and other fishermen, along the Atlantic coast in particular, has been so precarious for so many years that very few of them have any margin of safety. In fact I believe it could be stated that the great majority of them are living below the line of reasonable subsistence. That in my view is a fair statement of the case. Therefore they cannot absorb the results of a disaster; they are not in a position to do so, financially or otherwise. There should be no delay; parliament

Fishing Industry-Lobster Traps
should act. There has been a disaster. We all recognize it, and we fully sympathize with the victims. Let us act, and act quickly, effectively and directly in the matter, as under the constitution of Canada we have the power to do.

One in particular told me he was living on a farm that his grandfather had carved out of the wilderness. I asked him if he was eating all the fish he would like to eat, and he told me he could not buy the fish he would like to provide for his family because his overhead was too large and his income too small. That precluded any possibility of his buying the fish caught by the fishermen of Nova Scotia. I find the same thing true about the fishermen. They cannot buy the dairy products produced by the Ontario farmers. The Halifax Herald has been carrying numerous articles describing the suffering, misery and want that exists in Nova Scotia among the fishermen and miners.

are without fish while the fishermen are unable to buy the products of the forest. I am glad to know that there are many hon. members who are beginning to take cognizance of that fact. Do not start building roads with hand labour at this particular time of the year. I have had experience in that type of work. I have worked on some government projects put under way to ease the problems of the unemployed. I have in mind a particular project carried out in Calgary promoted by the previous government under the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. Barracks were built in Calgary at a cost of $1,250,000. The unemployed were given an opportunity to work with picks and shovels, and right beside them was an idle ditch digging machine. Was that used? No. How long did these men have an opportunity of working? After two or three weeks it was all over. Fifty per cent of the money they received was turned over to the city to pay arrears of taxes on the homes they owned. They were no better off when it was all over than they were when it started. Well, if it is six o'clock, all right, but this is rather an important matter. I am interested in it, and so is my constituency, but I am not going to delay the house with any extended remarks. I think we must cooperate with the government of Nova Scotia. While fisheries is a matter of federal concern and federal jurisdiction, the care of the fisherman and his family is a matter of civil and property rights, and for that reason the provincial government has a degree of responsibility. This government have from the outset laid down the policy that in matters of relief they must cooperate with the provincial governments. They have done so, and the provincial governments have paid to the fund one-half of the amount required. All I wish to say at this time is that I hope the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) will be generous in dealing with this matter, that he will continue his negotiations with the premier of Nova Scotia, and that he will see to it that whatever is necessary in the interests of the fishermen to protect and help them in this disaster will be done.
The Nova Scotia minister of public health comes from my own riding. His department is directly responsible for relief projects. I have discussed this matter with him several times, and I know they have difficulties. It is not just as easy as we think it is, talking here at a distance. But I believe that the minister of health of Nova Scotia is sympathetic to the fishermen, because he comes from the greatest fishing county in Canada; that the premier of Nova Scotia is deeply concerned in the condition of the fishermen, and that the federal government.will do their
